claim: More than two-thirds of excitatory inputs to D2-SPNs also target D1-SPNs.
source: Here using a G-deleted rabies system in mice, we found that more than two-thirds of excitatory inputs to D2-SPNs also target D1-SPNs, while only one-third do so vice versa.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings using the rabies-ChR2 system in brain slices, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: Only one-third of excitatory inputs to D1-SPNs target D2-SPNs.
source: Here using a G-deleted rabies system in mice, we found that more than two-thirds of excitatory inputs to D2-SPNs also target D1-SPNs, while only one-third do so vice versa.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings using the rabies-ChR2 system in brain slices, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of striatal D1- vs. D2-SPN-projecting cortical neurons differently regulate locomotion.
source: Optogenetic stimulation of striatal D1- vs. D2-SPN-projecting cortical neurons differently regulate locomotion, reinforcement learning, and sequence behavior, implying the functional dichotomy of pathway-specific corticostriatal subcircuits.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo optogenetic experiments in open field tests, as shown in Figure 3.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of striatal D1- vs. D2-SPN-projecting cortical neurons differently regulate reinforcement learning.
source: Optogenetic stimulation of striatal D1- vs. D2-SPN-projecting cortical neurons differently regulate locomotion, reinforcement learning, and sequence behavior, implying the functional dichotomy of pathway-specific corticostriatal subcircuits.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo optogenetic experiments in intracranial self-stimulation (ICSS) tests, as shown in Figure 3.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of striatal D1- vs. D2-SPN-projecting cortical neurons differently regulate sequence behavior.
source: Optogenetic stimulation of striatal D1- vs. D2-SPN-projecting cortical neurons differently regulate locomotion, reinforcement learning, and sequence behavior, implying the functional dichotomy of pathway-specific corticostriatal subcircuits.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo optogenetic experiments during FR8 sequence tasks, as shown in Figure 4.

claim: Corticostriatal circuits are critically involved in sensory, cognition, and the learning and control of actions.
source: The corticostriatal circuits are critically involved in sensory, cognition, and the learning and control of actions (Aoki et al., 2019; Graybiel, 1998; Haber, 2016; Hikosaka et al., 1998; Jin and Costa, 2010; Jin and Costa, 2015; Kupferschmidt et al., 2017; Stephenson-Jones et al., 2011; Tanji, 2001; Yin and Knowlton, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Dysfunctional corticostriatal circuitry has been implicated in numerous neurological and psychiatric diseases.
source: Dysfunctional corticostriatal circuitry has been implicated in numerous neurological and psychiatric diseases (Shepherd, 2013), including Parkinson's (Redgrave et al., 2010), autism (Monteiro and Feng, 2017), and obsessive-compulsive disorder (Dalley and Robbins, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The striatal direct and indirect pathways constitute the core components for basal ganglia functions in relation to action learning and movement control.
source: The striatal direct and indirect pathways, made up of D1- vs. D2-expressing spiny projection neurons (SPNs) respectively, constitute the core components for basal ganglia functions in relation to action learning and movement control (Albin et al., 1989; DeLong, 1990; Gerfen et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The two pathways play distinct yet complementary roles in controlling actions.
source: Numerous studies have suggested that the two pathways play distinct yet complementary roles in controlling actions (Cui et al., 2013; Geddes et al., 2018; Hikosaka et al., 2019; Hikosaka et al., 2000; Jin et al., 2014; Kravitz et al., 2010; Markowitz et al., 2018; Mink, 2003; Tecuapetla et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: D1- and D2-SPNs are spatially intermixed in the striatum.
source: It is well known that D1- and D2-SPNs are spatially intermixed in the striatum, and they both receive major excitatory inputs from the cerebral cortex (Bolam et al., 2000; Pan et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and is considered established knowledge.

claim: D1- and D2-SPNs both receive major excitatory inputs from the cerebral cortex.
source: It is well known that D1- and D2-SPNs are spatially intermixed in the striatum, and they both receive major excitatory inputs from the cerebral cortex (Bolam et al., 2000; Pan et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and is considered established knowledge.

claim: Sensory and limbic cortical regions preferably send projections to D1-SPNs, compared to the motor cortical inputs biased toward D2-SPNs.
source: A previous monosynaptic rabies tracing study has revealed that sensory and limbic cortical regions preferably send projections to D1-SPNs, compared to the motor cortical inputs biased toward D2-SPNs (Wall et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Recordings from mCherry-negative, non-starter striatal D1-SPNs in striatal D1-rabies-ChR2-infected mice revealed that with high probability (~63%) a D1-SPN receives the inputs from the presynaptic excitatory neurons projecting to surrounding D1-SPNs.
source: Recordings from the mCherry-negative, non-starter striatal D1-SPNs in striatal D1-rabies-ChR2-infected mice revealed that with high probability (~63%) a D1-SPN receives the inputs from the presynaptic excitatory neurons projecting to surrounding D1-SPNs (Figure 2B and D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 2B and D.

claim: Recordings from mCherry-negative non-starter striatal D2-SPNs in striatal D2-rabies-ChR2-tracing mice revealed that with a very high probability (~79%) a D2-SPN receives the inputs from the presynaptic excitatory neurons that project to surrounding D2-SPNs.
source: Similarly, recordings from mCherry-negative non-starter striatal D2-SPNs in striatal D2-rabies-ChR2-tracing mice revealed that with a very high probability (~79%) a D2-SPN receives the inputs from the presynaptic excitatory neurons that project to surrounding D2-SPNs (Figure 2C and D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Recordings from striatal D2-SPNs in the striatal D1-rabies-ChR2-tracing mice revealed that the chance for a D2-SPN to receive excitatory inputs from the presynaptic neurons projecting to surrounding D1-SPNs is rather low (~40%).
source: However, recordings from striatal D2-SPNs in the striatal D1-rabies-ChR2-tracing mice revealed that the chance for a D2-SPN to receive excitatory inputs from the presynaptic neurons projecting to surrounding D1-SPNs is rather low (~40%, Figure 2E and G; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 2E and G.

claim: Recordings from striatal D1-SPNs in the striatal D2-rabies-ChR2-tracing mice revealed that the chance for a D1-SPN to receive the excitatory inputs from the presynaptic neurons projecting to surrounding D2-SPNs is remarkably high (~73%).
source: In contrast, recordings from striatal D1-SPNs in the striatal D2-rabies-ChR2-tracing mice revealed that the chance for a D1-SPN to receive the excitatory inputs from the presynaptic neurons projecting to surrounding D2-SPNs is remarkably high (~73%, Figure 2F and G; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: The likelihood that the input connectivity was significantly higher from the presynaptic excitatory inputs of D2-SPNs to D1-SPNs than from the presynaptic excitatory inputs of D1-SPNs to D2-SPNs.
source: Notably, the likelihood that the input connectivity was significantly higher from the presynaptic excitatory inputs of D2-SPNs to D1-SPNs than from the presynaptic excitatory inputs of D1-SPNs to D2-SPNs (Figure 2D and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 2D and G.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation (20 Hz) of D1-SPNs in the DMS or DLS facilitated locomotion.
source: Consistent with the previous observations (Kravitz et al., 2010), optogenetic stimulation (20 Hz) of D1-SPNs in the DMS or DLS facilitated locomotion (Figure 3B, C, E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from open field tests shown in Figure 3B, C, E and F, and is consistent with previous research.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation (20 Hz) of D2-SPNs in DMS significantly suppressed locomotion.
source: Conversely, optogenetic stimulation (20 Hz) of D2-SPNs in DMS significantly suppressed locomotion (Figure 3B and D), which is less obvious in DLS (Figure 3E and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from open field tests shown in Figure 3B and D.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation (20 Hz) of D2-SPNs in DLS does not significantly suppress locomotion.
source: Conversely, optogenetic stimulation (20 Hz) of D2-SPNs in DMS significantly suppressed locomotion (Figure 3B and D), which is less obvious in DLS (Figure 3E and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from open field tests shown in Figure 3E and G.

claim: High-frequency (20 Hz) but not low-frequency (5 Hz) optogenetic stimulation of MCC neurons that project to D1-SPNs significantly facilitated locomotion in the open field.
source: Notably, high-frequency (20 Hz) but not low-frequency (5 Hz) optogenetic stimulation of MCC neurons that project to D1-SPNs significantly facilitated locomotion in the open field (Figure 3H, I; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), similar to D1-SPN activation in DMS.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from open field tests shown in Figure 3H, I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation (20 Hz) of D2-SPN projecting MCC neurons in the same location did not alter locomotion in the open field.
source: However, optogenetic stimulation (20 Hz) of D2-SPN projecting MCC neurons in the same location did not alter locomotion in the open field (Figure 3H and J), in contrast with the effects of stimulation of D2-SPNs in DMS (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from open field tests shown in Figure 3H and J.

claim: High-frequency optogenetic stimulation (20 Hz) of M1 neurons that project to D1-SPNs facilitated locomotion in the open field.
source: Similarly, high-frequency optogenetic stimulation (20 Hz) of M1 neurons that project to D1-SPNs facilitated locomotion in the open field (Figure 3K and L; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), while 20 Hz stimulation of the M1 neurons projecting to D2-SPNs did not significantly alter locomotion (Figure 3K and M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from open field tests shown in Figure 3K and L.

claim: 20 Hz stimulation of the M1 neurons projecting to D2-SPNs did not significantly alter locomotion.
source: Similarly, high-frequency optogenetic stimulation (20 Hz) of M1 neurons that project to D1-SPNs facilitated locomotion in the open field (Figure 3K and L; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), while 20 Hz stimulation of the M1 neurons projecting to D2-SPNs did not significantly alter locomotion (Figure 3K and M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from open field tests shown in Figure 3K and M.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of D1-SPNs robustly supported intracranial self-stimulation (ICSS) in either DMS or DLS.
source: We first performed experiments in the D1-Cre mice with viral expression of ChR2 in the striatum and found that optogenetic stimulation of D1-SPNs robustly supported intracranial self-stimulation (ICSS; Figure 3N) in either DMS (Figure 3O) or DLS (Figure 3P).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ICSS tests shown in Figure 3O and P.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of D2-SPNs, either in DMS or DLS, did not promote ICSS behavior.
source: Conversely, optogenetic stimulation of D2-SPNs, either in DMS (Figure 3O) or DLS (Figure 3P), did not promote ICSS behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ICSS tests shown in Figure 3O and P.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of striatal D1-SPN projecting neurons was sufficient to support ICSS behavior both in MCC and in M1.
source: Similar to the effects of direct striatal D1-SPN stimulation (Figure 3O and P), optogenetic stimulation of striatal D1-SPN projecting neurons was sufficient to support ICSS behavior both in MCC (Figure 3Q and R) and in M1 (Figure 3Q and S).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ICSS tests shown in Figure 3Q, R and S.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of the cortical neurons projecting to D2-SPNs also significantly drove ICSS behavior, irrespective of whether it is in MCC or M1.
source: Notably, optogenetic stimulation of the cortical neurons projecting to D2-SPNs also significantly drove ICSS behavior, irrespective of whether it is in MCC (Figure 3R) or M1 (Figure 3S).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ICSS tests shown in Figure 3R and S.

claim: Corticostriatal circuitry is critical for action sequence learning and execution.
source: Corticostriatal circuitry is critical for action sequence learning and execution (Geddes et al., 2018; Hikosaka et al., 1998; Jin and Costa, 2010; Jin and Costa, 2015; Jin et al., 2014; Tanji, 2001; Tecuapetla et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Striatal direct and indirect pathways have been suggested to play distinct roles in controlling learned action sequences, as D1-SPNs facilitate ongoing actions while D2-SPNs inhibit actions and mediate switching.
source: In particular, striatal direct and indirect pathways have been suggested to play distinct roles in controlling learned action sequences, as D1-SPNs facilitate ongoing actions while D2-SPNs inhibit actions and mediate switching (Geddes et al., 2018; Jin and Costa, 2010; Jin and Costa, 2015; Jin et al., 2014; Tecuapetla et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Stimulation of MCC inputs to D1-SPNs facilitated lever pressing over the duration of the FR8 sequence.
source: Stimulation of MCC inputs to D1-SPNs facilitated lever pressing over the duration of the FR8 sequence (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from FR8 sequence tasks shown in Figure 4B and D.

claim: Stimulation of MCC inputs to D2-SPNs slightly reduced the lever press rate over the stimulation period.
source: Conversely, stimulation of MCC inputs to D2-SPNs slightly reduced the lever press rate over the stimulation period (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from FR8 sequence tasks shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The modulation effects on lever pressing rate were significantly different between optogenetic stimulation of D1- and D2-SPN projecting MCC neurons.
source: The modulation effects on lever pressing rate were significantly different between optogenetic stimulation of D1- and D2-SPN projecting MCC neurons (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from FR8 sequence tasks shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Optogenetic activation of the M1 neurons that project to D1-SPNs facilitated lever pressing during sequence execution.
source: On the other hand, optogenetic activation of the M1 neurons that project to D1-SPNs facilitated lever pressing during sequence execution (Figure 4F and H), similar to the effects of MCC stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from FR8 sequence tasks shown in Figure 4F and H.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of the M1 neurons projecting to D2-SPNs delivered an overall facilitation effect on lever pressing.
source: However, optogenetic stimulation of the M1 neurons projecting to D2-SPNs delivered an overall facilitation effect on lever pressing (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from FR8 sequence tasks shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: Stimulation of either D1- or D2-SPN projecting M1 neurons facilitated lever pressing to a similar degree.
source: Overall, stimulation of either D1- or D2-SPN projecting M1 neurons facilitated lever pressing to a similar degree (Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from FR8 sequence tasks shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The excitatory inputs to D1-SPNs mostly control the striatal direct pathway.
source: Based on this asymmetrically overlapping functional organization, one would predict that the excitatory inputs to D1-SPNs mostly control the striatal direct pathway, while the inputs to D2-SPNs would drive both the indirect and direct pathways (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the connectivity data and supported by the behavioral experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: The inputs to D2-SPNs would drive both the indirect and direct pathways.
source: Based on this asymmetrically overlapping functional organization, one would predict that the excitatory inputs to D1-SPNs mostly control the striatal direct pathway, while the inputs to D2-SPNs would drive both the indirect and direct pathways (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the connectivity data and supported by the behavioral experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: The cortical neurons in the same cortical layer and spatial location could differently control actions depending on their striatal projection targets, in a pathway- and cell type-specific manner.
source: It thus rules out the possibility that the behavioral effects observed by cortical stimulation in the rabies-ChR2 mice were triggered through direct striatal activation due to the light penetration into the striatum. These results are consistent with the functional connectivity in which the excitatory inputs to D1-SPNs mostly drive the direct pathway, and the inputs to D2-SPNs target both the indirect and direct pathways (Figure 3A). It also suggests that the cortical neurons in the same cortical layer and spatial location could differently control actions depending on their striatal projection targets, in a pathway- and cell type-specific manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from optogenetic behavioral experiments and is inferred from the results.

claim: Intensive labeling was found in different cortical regions including the midcingulate cortex (MCC) and the primary motor cortex (M1) in both D1- and A2a-Cre tracing experiments.
source: In both D1- and A2a-Cre tracing experiments, intensive labeling was found in different cortical regions as expected, including the midcingulate cortex (MCC; van Heukelum et al., 2020; Vogt and Paxinos, 2014) and the primary motor cortex (M1), which targets mainly the dorsal medial and dorsal lateral striatum, respectively (Aoki et al., 2019; Bolam et al., 2000; Pan et al., 2010; Shepherd, 2013; Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from rabies tracing shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: MCC targets mainly the dorsal medial striatum.
source: In both D1- and A2a-Cre tracing experiments, intensive labeling was found in different cortical regions as expected, including the midcingulate cortex (MCC; van Heukelum et al., 2020; Vogt and Paxinos, 2014) and the primary motor cortex (M1), which targets mainly the dorsal medial and dorsal lateral striatum, respectively (Aoki et al., 2019; Bolam et al., 2000; Pan et al., 2010; Shepherd, 2013; Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from rabies tracing shown in Figure 1C and D, and is consistent with previous research.

claim: M1 targets mainly the dorsal lateral striatum.
source: In both D1- and A2a-Cre tracing experiments, intensive labeling was found in different cortical regions as expected, including the midcingulate cortex (MCC; van Heukelum et al., 2020; Vogt and Paxinos, 2014) and the primary motor cortex (M1), which targets mainly the dorsal medial and dorsal lateral striatum, respectively (Aoki et al., 2019; Bolam et al., 2000; Pan et al., 2010; Shepherd, 2013; Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from rabies tracing shown in Figure 1C and D, and is consistent with previous research.

claim: Both the current-voltage relationship and the spiking activity confirmed the overall health and the functional expression of ChR2 in the rabies-infected cortical neurons.
source: Both the current-voltage relationship revealed by somatic current injections (Figure 1H) and the spiking activity elicited by blue laser frequency stimulation (Figure 1I; Figure 1—figure supplement 1) confirmed the overall health and the functional expression of ChR2 in the rabies-infected cortical neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings shown in Figure 1H, I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The cortical neurons projecting to striatum mainly consist of layer 2/3 and layer 5 pyramidal cells.
source: The cortical neurons projecting to striatum mainly consist of layer 2/3 and layer 5 pyramidal cells (Klug et al., 2018; Wall et al., 2013), including both the intratelencephalic (IT) and pyramidal tract (PT) types of neurons (Shepherd, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Both the striatal direct and indirect pathways receive functional inputs from both the IT and PT neurons.
source: While some anatomical preference might exist (Lei et al., 2004), it has been found that both the striatal direct and indirect pathways receive functional inputs from both the IT and PT neurons (Ballion et al., 2008; Kress et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Both striatal direct and indirect pathways receive inhibitory inputs from certain GABAergic interneurons in motor cortices.
source: In addition, it has been known that both striatal direct and indirect pathways receive inhibitory inputs from certain GABAergic interneurons in motor cortices (Melzer et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The traditional model of the basal ganglia suggests that the direct and indirect pathways play opposing roles in facilitating and inhibiting action, respectively.
source: The traditional model of the basal ganglia suggests that the direct and indirect pathways play opposing roles in facilitating and inhibiting action, respectively (Albin et al., 1989; DeLong, 1990; Kravitz et al., 2010), although one study (Cui et al., 2021) reported an alternative pattern, which may stem from differences in stimulation coordinates and fiber-optic diameter.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: More recent models of basal ganglia propose that the direct pathway co-activates and cooperates with the indirect pathway, with the former activating the selected action and the latter inhibiting the competing actions.
source: More recent models of basal ganglia, however, propose that the direct pathway co-activates and cooperates with the indirect pathway, with the former activating the selected action and the latter inhibiting the competing actions (Cui et al., 2013; Hikosaka et al., 2000; Jin et al., 2014; Mink, 1996; Tecuapetla et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The striatal D1- and D2-SPNs are co-activated during the initiation of an action sequence but become largely segregated during the sequence performance.
source: Under more complicated behavior context, it has been previously reported that the striatal D1- and D2-SPNs are co-activated during the initiation of an action sequence but become largely segregated during the sequence performance (Geddes et al., 2018; Jin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The various subpopulations of striatal D1- and D2-SPNs differently change their firing activity to support the start/stop of the sequence, the execution of the elemental actions, and the switch between subsequences.
source: More specifically, the various subpopulations of striatal D1- and D2-SPNs differently change their firing activity to support the start/stop of the sequence, the execution of the elemental actions, and the switch between subsequences (Geddes et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The striatal direct and indirect pathways have to dynamically coordinate their activity throughout the performance of sequential actions.
source: These previous findings thus suggested that the striatal direct and indirect pathways have to dynamically coordinate their activity throughout the performance of sequential actions (Geddes et al., 2018; Hikosaka et al., 2019; Jin and Costa, 2015; Markowitz et al., 2018; Tecuapetla et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and is inferred from previous findings.

claim: The largely segregated but asymmetrically overlapping organization of the cortical projections to striatal direct vs. indirect pathway provides a structural foundation for the striatal direct and indirect pathways to implement dynamic coordination of activity during sequence behavior.
source: This specific corticostriatal organization provides a structural foundation for the striatal direct and indirect pathways to implement such a dynamic coordination of activity during sequence behavior (Geddes et al., 2018; Hikosaka et al., 2019; Hikosaka et al., 1998; Jin and Costa, 2010; Jin and Costa, 2015; Jin et al., 2014; Markowitz et al., 2018; Tanji, 2001; Tecuapetla et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental findings and supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The dedicated cortical projections to striatal direct vs. indirect pathway are well suited for controlling sequence initiation and termination, where the activation of D1- and D2-SPNs is critical.
source: For instance, the dedicated cortical projections to striatal direct vs. indirect pathway are well suited for controlling sequence initiation and termination, where the activation of D1- and D2-SPNs is critical (DeLong, 1990; Geddes et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental findings and supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The overlapping cortical projections to both striatal direct and indirect pathways could be crucial for action switching, which requires proper coordination of the two pathways to inhibit current action and activate the upcoming one.
source: On the other hand, the overlapping cortical projections to both striatal direct and indirect pathways could be crucial for action switching, which requires proper coordination of the two pathways to inhibit current action and activate the upcoming one (DeLong, 1990; Geddes et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental findings and supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The striatal D1- vs. D2-SPN projecting neurons in the cerebral cortex would fire differently but activate in relation with each other during behavior.
source: Our findings also predict that the striatal D1- vs. D2-SPN projecting neurons in the cerebral cortex would fire differently but activate in relation with each other during behavior.
evidence: This claim is a prediction inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: Corticospinal neurons, which project to both spinal cord and DLS, form uneven synapses onto direct and indirect pathway neurons in the DLS and preferentially target D1- other than D2-SPNs.
source: However, the overall functional organization does imply that while the excitatory inputs to D1-SPNs in general drive the striatal direct pathway, the excitatory inputs to D2-SPNs control both the striatal direct and indirect pathways. Indeed, it has been recently reported that corticospinal neurons, which project to both spinal cord and DLS, form uneven synapses onto direct and indirect pathway neurons in the DLS and preferentially target D1- other than D2-SPNs (Nelson et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: Sustained optogenetic stimulation (500 ms) of ChR2-expressing presynaptic terminals induces transient, rather than sustained, action potential firing on the postsynaptic neurons.
source: However, a previous optogenetic study on thalamo-cortical synapses (Cruikshank et al., 2010) demonstrated that sustained optogenetic stimulation (500 ms) of ChR2-expressing presynaptic terminals induces transient, rather than sustained, action potential firing on the postsynaptic neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The behavioral effects of optogenetic stimulation are most likely driven by the excitation of ChR2-expressing D1- or D2-SPN projecting neurons in the targeted cortical area, rather than by efferent terminals from neurons located outside this region.
source: Considering the much longer stimulation durations used in our optogenetic experiments (15 s for open-field, 1 s for ICSS, and 8 s for the FR8/FR4), it provides compelling evidence that the behavioral effects of optogenetic stimulation are most likely driven by the excitation of ChR2-expressing D1- or D2-SPN projecting neurons in the targeted cortical area, rather than by efferent terminals from neurons located outside this region.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental design and supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: All procedures were approved by the Salk Institute Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC; protocol 12–00032) and followed NIH guidelines for the care and use of laboratory animals.
source: All procedures were approved by the Salk Institute Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC; protocol 12–00032) and followed NIH guidelines for the care and use of laboratory animals.
evidence: This is a statement of ethical compliance.

claim: Group-housed male and female mice (2–6 months old) were used in this study.
source: Group-housed male and female mice (2–6 months old) were used in this study.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: Animals were housed on a 12 hr dark/12 hr light cycle (dark from 6 pm to 6 am).
source: Animals were housed on a 12 hr dark/12 hr light cycle (dark from 6 pm to 6 am).
evidence: This is a description of the housing conditions.

claim: Heterozygous Drd1-Cre and Adora2a-Cre mice were obtained from MMRRC and were backcrossed to C57BL/6 J mice (>9 generations).
source: Heterozygous Drd1-Cre (The Jackson Laboratory, stock # 030329, GENSAT: EY217) and Adora2a-Cre (The Jackson Laboratory, stock # 036158, GENSAT: KG139) mice were obtained from MMRRC and were backcrossed to C57BL/6 J mice, stock # 000664 (>9 generations; Cui et al., 2013; Jin et al., 2014; Madisen et al., 2012; Tecuapetla et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of the mouse lines used.

claim: BAC reporter lines D1-eGFP and D2-eGFP were crossed to Drd1-Cre (D1-Cre) and Adora2a-Cre (A2a-Cre) mice to identify D1- and D2-SPNs for electrophysiological recordings.
source: BAC reporter lines D1-eGFP (MMRRC: MMRRC_000297-MU; GENSAT: X60) and D2-eGFP (MMRRC: MMRRC_00230-UNC; GENSAT: S118; Gong et al., 2007) were crossed to Drd1-Cre (D1-Cre) and Adora2a-Cre (A2a-Cre) mice to identify D1- and D2-SPNs for electrophysiological recordings.
evidence: This is a description of the mouse lines used for recordings.

claim: 4–8 days were allowed for expression and optimal cell health post unilateral (EnvA) SAD-∆G Rabies-ChR2-mCherry injection before electrophysiology recordings on acute slice were carried out.
source: 4–8 days were allowed for expression and optimal cell health post unilateral (EnvA) SAD-∆G Rabies-ChR2-mCherry injection before electrophysiology recordings on acute slice were carried out (Klug et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental timeline.

claim: A cell is considered connected if it has a detectable, reliable current (20 sweeps, 0.05 Hz) with onset latency less than 10 ms post laser-on.
source: A cell is considered connected if it has a detectable, reliable current (20 sweeps, 0.05 Hz) with onset latency less than 10 ms post laser-on (Klug et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of the criteria for determining functional connectivity.

claim: Fisher's exact test was used in comparing the likelihood of connections in slice recordings.
source: Fisher's exact test was used in comparing the likelihood of connections in slice recordings.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical method used.

claim: Student unpaired two-tailed t-test was used in open field test and sequence operant task to analyze optogenetic stimulation effects.
source: Student unpaired two-tailed t-test was used in open field test and sequence operant task to analyze optogenetic stimulation effects.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical method used.

claim: The reinforcing effect of each group in the ICSS task was assessed using a permutation test (10,000 permutations per group).
source: The reinforcing effect of each group in the ICSS task was assessed using a permutation test (10,000 permutations per group).
evidence: This is a description of the statistical method used.
